title: What happened? The Spread of Fake News Publisher Content During the 2016 U.S. Presidential Election
screen_reason: Analysis of a daily uniform-random sample of tweets mentioning Trump or Clinton (May 2014 - Jan 2017), with every external URL resolved and classified at the publisher level as fake or traditional news. The paper defines and reports a fake-news content fraction f = |fake-publisher tweets| / (|fake| + |traditional| publisher tweets) and gives its level at three campaign moments (about 20% / ~30% / ~40%), i.e. a share of shared news links that came from fake news publishers - a SHARING (content_share) estimate with a stated denominator.

estimates.country: Not specified for the Twitter sample (tweets mentioning 'Trump' or 'Clinton', no geographic filter); the subject matter is the 2016 U.S. Presidential election and the linked Gallup interviews are U.S. national
estimates.date: Tweet collection May 23, 2014 - January 1, 2017; the prevalence time series in Figure 2 runs June-November 2016
estimates.measure_type: % of candidate-related tweet shares of news-publisher links that pointed to a fake news publisher (rather than a traditional news publisher), at the post-nomination stage of the 2016 campaign
estimates.value_raw: the average fraction of fake news content is about 20% before the conventions, it lies at ~ 30% after the nominations and reaches ~ 40% right before the election
estimates.denominator: Tweets mentioning a candidate that contain an external link to EITHER a fake news publisher OR a traditional news publisher on the same day (f = |F| / (|F| + |T|)). Underlying corpus: 5,000 Trump-keyword and 5,000 Clinton-keyword tweets uniformly randomly sampled per day; after filtering to tweets with external URLs, 3,072,251 shares of 1,529,251 unique shortened URLs (Trump) and 4,689,087 shares of 2,025,203 unique URLs (Clinton); restricted to the news domain lists, ~270K unique articles shared in ~564K Trump tweets and ~350K unique articles in 1.1M Clinton tweets
estimates.definition: The tweet's external link resolved to a web domain on the Allcott, Gentzkow & Yu (2019) fake-news publisher list (a union of five lists: Grinberg et al. 490 publishers, PolitiFact 325, BuzzFeed 223, Guess et al. 92, and FactCheck)
estimates.misinfo_def: Publisher-level definition, quoting Lazer et al.: "focusing on the original sources - the publishers - rather than individual stories, because we view the defining element of fake news to be the intent and processes of the publisher"
estimates.n: Tweets containing fake- or traditional-publisher links about the candidates (~564K Trump tweets and ~1.1M Clinton tweets contained articles from the two domain sets)
estimates.source_quote: 20% before the conventions, it lies at ≈ 30% after the nominations
estimates.page_loc: Section 6, 'Changes in Fake News Production and Consumption', p. 143; Figure 2
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Fake news publishers taken from Allcott, Gentzkow & Yu (2019), a union of five external lists (Grinberg et al. 490 publishers; PolitiFact's guide 325; three BuzzFeed articles 223 sites; Guess et al. 92; FactCheck's list), chosen for widest coverage and for the authors' robustness checks (requiring 2-3 list agreement, and dropping any one of the five lists). Traditional news = the 5,497 domains in Alexa's news category minus the fake set. No article-level verification; the authors note in Limitations that 'domains classified as fake at times might publish reliable news' and that mainstream sites can also disseminate misinformation.
estimates.moderator_quote: Next, fake news content fraction for Clinton and Trump tweets are measured as fClinton,i = |FClinton,i| / (|FClinton,i| + |TClinton,i|) and fTrump,i = |FTrump,i| / (|FTrump,i| + |TTrump,i|) respectively.
estimates.notes: TIME SERIES COLLAPSED to one representative point: I took the ~30% post-nomination level, i.e. the general-election campaign, as representative; the series runs about 20% pre-convention up to about 40% immediately before election day. Two caveats an adjudicator should weigh. (a) All three values are approximations the author reads off a 15-day centred moving average in Figure 2, not tabulated numbers. (b) The sentence does not say whether the three values describe the Clinton series, the Trump series, or both; the preceding clause ('more so for Clinton tweets but also for Trump tweets') and the y-axis range of Figure 2 (0.1-0.4) suggest the ~40% endpoint is the Clinton curve, so the true Trump-tweet level is lower. The DENOMINATOR is the critical moderator here: it is news-publisher links only (fake + traditional), NOT all tweets and not all URLs, so this figure is much larger than a share-of-all-content estimate would be. Quote trimmed to the single verbatim line carrying the value; the sentence's opening ('Figure 2 also shows an increasing popularity of fake news producers over time... While the average fraction of fake news content is about') sits on the preceding print line, which the .txt rendering interleaves with a table. platform_norm corrected from 'Twitter' to the controlled value 'Twitter/X'.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) 'the number of users sharing traditional news content outnumbered those that share content produced by fake news outlets roughly one to four' would imply about 20% of news-sharing users, but it is an approximate RATIO and converting it to a share is exactly the derived-complement computation R8 forbids, so no row. (2) CONCENTRATION: the paper devotes a subsection and Figure 1 to how popularity concentrates across publishers, but never states a top-group % paired with that group's share of activity. What it gives - '68% and 61% of fake news publishers had popularity strictly less than 100 for Trump and Clinton respectively. These numbers are 84% and 81% for traditional news publishers' and 'there are no fake news publishers that single-handedly garnered more than 30K shares' - is a CCDF over domains, which fails R1 (no conc_group_pct/conc_share_pct pair). The paper's other concentration statement, 'only 1% of individuals accounted for 80% of fake news source exposures', is quoted from Grinberg et al. and excluded by R8. (3) Per-article popularity (traditional articles shared by 2.8 users on average vs 2.88 for fake; 4.7 vs 5.5 days) are counts of shares per article, not a misinformation share of anything. (4) Topic composition inside each publisher class (election = 48% of traditional vs 24% of fake shares; emails = 31% of fake vs 16% of traditional shares) describes agenda, not falsity, so R3 does not apply. (5) Candidate focus (e.g. '48% of shares of fake news sources on the election were mentioning Clinton') is likewise composition, not prevalence. (6) The whole 'fake news exposure' section (Section 8) measures word-level alignment between Gallup interview responses and fake-news vocabulary (a log-odds Z-score 'fake-ness'), not a share of respondents exposed; the Gallup data therefore yield NO recall row despite the section title. (7) Tone results (mean net positivity -1.3 for fake vs 2.2 for traditional) are scale means. (8) COUNTRY JUDGEMENT CALL: country_norm = Global because the tweet sample is keyword-defined with no geographic restriction and the paper never states a country for it; an adjudicator who codes by subject matter (a U.S. election, U.S. domain lists, U.S. Gallup panel) would code United States / single instead, and I would not object.

rob.design: Observational. Twitter: tweets sampled uniformly at random at the daily level through Sysomos MAP, 5,000/day containing 'Trump' and 5,000/day containing 'Clinton', 23 May 2014 - 1 January 2017 (~4.8M tweets per candidate); tweets without an external URL dropped, shortened URLs resolved and page content extracted (~1.7M unique URLs); Twitter-internal URLs removed. Classification is source-level: fake-news publishers from Allcott, Gentzkow & Yu (2019) (union of five lists, with the authors' own robustness checks at 2-of-5 and 3-of-5 list agreement and leave-one-list-out); traditional news = Alexa's 5,497 news-category domains minus the fake set. No inter-coder reliability applies (list matching). Topic modelling via guided LDA with expert seed words, validated on Amazon Mechanical Turk (15 of 19 topics F1 >= 0.75). Gallup Daily survey: ~500 US adults aged 18+ per day across all 50 states and DC, ~60% cellphone / 40% landline, 11 July - 7 November 2016, weekly margin of sampling error +/-2 points at 95%, post-stratification weights used. Stated limitations: domain-level labels mis-classify individual articles in both directions; only articles shared at least once on Twitter are observed, so production and consumption cannot be separated; Twitter users are not representative of the US population; all findings are correlational.
